review_text_for_llm:
Golf it! stands out on its own as a unique entry to the mini-golf series. It does have a skill check as you need to manually set the power of your ball by flicking your mouse back and forth. It takes some time to get used to but feels great once its working and the ability to make very fine tuned shots becomes limitless. An already strong contender bolstered by its amazingly skilled map making community and workshop integration. Finally the custom hosting settings allow for use of different clubs, hole and one and friction changes allowing for varied play on the same course.

This to me is the successor to Golf with Friends.

As of Update v1.0 -
The skill check can be mitigated by using a controller and the new power system which is very reminiscent of Golf With Friends. I prefer it though as it allows you to go pass the 'max' power so you have the freedom to do the same type of shot a mouse/keyboard player would.

review_text_for_llm:
It's great fun!

As of writing, I spent 464 hours ingame, roughly 150+ hours in the editor. If you ask me, it's the better of the two major fun golf games out there, but I own both anyway. It's minigolf, get it, it's fun! :3 

There are incredible fun and well made custom maps, super creative stuff. Teams create elaborate 50+ hole maps or psychedelic theme parks. Some maps feel more like adventure games than minigolf. It's amazing. But also the mechanic just feels better. "Hitting" your ball by moving your mouse is just more interesting than see a bar go bloop. You can play with additional help, and alternate shooting modes if needed, but being frustrated at your own failure to move the mouse just a tad different is just as much fun, as it is to nail the perfect hole-in-one! 

I'd easily recommend the game, especially with friends or on stream. Just be sure to talk to the map community and look up stuff on youtube for help if you want to create your own course. The editor is intuitive, but some things just need to be learnt, also undo/redo is still wonky and the more creative stuff needs expert help :D Still, it's an easy recommend as said.

Conclusion: Age of Defence does not even come close to Warstone.

Sure, there is a really good game somewhere underneath this mess, but there is still an awful lot of work to be done.
Should never have left early access in this state...

This game is a hidden gem

Don't be put off by the roguelike tag if you're not into roguelikes. It has clear progression, despite dying and having to do another run.

You basically spend your time going through a run with random gen maps. A bunch of different classes allow you to play the game in a drastically different style with each one.
Characters don't lose equipment and are not permadeath.

This game is all about long-term progression, regularly unlocking new skills, new improvements, new equipment. You start out "weak", and while you level up you really feel the difference.

Overall this game has taken me away from all others, and I suspect that will be the case for a long time. It's outrageously fun.

I've not tried multiplayer yet, but it's a feature, that also looks great.

review_text_for_llm:
This is an early access game masquerading as a full launch. It's a decent rogue-lite with an insanely shallow gameplay loop. While the town building is fun and leveling classes to 20 is an ok experience, there just isn't enough content to justify a ~$20 price tag. There are still insane balance issues, and the game definitely needs to add a lot more gear/items/trinkets/upgrades to make the NG+ grind feel worthwhile. 

It's also been over a month and we still have yet to see anything added besides a few minor tweaks and bug fixes. I'd suggest waiting at least 6 months to a year before giving this a go. It has a potential, but right now, not enough to make it worthwhile.

Edit: It's now 9 months since launch with zero additional content added besides bug fixes and balancing. Unfortunately, this game is not worth $18 in its current state and the devs refuse to explain what actual content they will add, if any, and whether or not it will be free or paid DLC. Which is sad, because the gameplay loop is fun. If you can snag it at a DEEP discount (like 75% or more), it'd be worth it.

review_text_for_llm:
When the game first came out and all the players were of a low level it was extremely fun, one of the best drop-in multiplayer games I've ever played. 
But then within a few weeks everyone was higher level and at higher level the game changes from a tense but fast paced dungeon crawler with deeply required teamwork and roleplay (combat wise) into; everyone is a flourescent pink flashing anime character with lasers shooting out of their orifices in every direction and tearing across the map by themselves at the speed of light obliterating hordes of enemies and in an instant breaking the setting, the atmosphere and the gameplay.
If the developers could capture the essence of that early game experience, perhaps cap player movement speed harder (and naturally slow down enemies/missiles etc in turn) and remove the pink powerup laser system I think they would be most of the way to making the game what it could be. But as it stands I'm not interested.

review_text_for_llm:
This game reminds me a bit of others like Everyone Has Gone to the Rapture, or The Vanishing of Ethan Carter. There's a lot of mystery for you to uncover, a lot of walking (or in this case biking,) and very little in the way of gameplay. Aside from biking around, you just take pictures, record audio, and chat with the occasional NPC. 

If that's not your thing, you probably won't find much to enjoy here. This game is entirely driven by emotion, feeling of grief, love, the struggles of comprehending the past and present, while fearing for the future. It's also accompanied by gorgeous visuals and a unique art style, and a beautiful score. I guess I'd also compare it heavily to the Life is Strange games, although I think pacing is not on this game's side. Maybe it should've been shorter, but I have a hard time thinking of playing this game again, unless it's been long enough that I forgot what happens. 

So, I guess for a first time playthrough, I'd recommend it. I'd say it's worth the price if you want to go through every inch of this beautiful world.

review_text_for_llm:
A real gem of a game, there should be more relaxing games that focus on exploration, contemplation and peace of mind rather than violence and killing. 

A coming of age story worthy of a grand novel, telling of the change in the world, exploring a post-age world where man and nature once again reevaluate their relationship, will it once again be a cycle of war and destruction or one of hope and betterment? With your handy voice recorder, Polaroid and diary, you set off to find out about the larger world and also perhaps oneself.

The shaded cell art style lends to the whimsical yet serious nature of the narrative, the voice acting are spot on and the vistas are well thought off to evoke a sense of nostalgia, mystery and wonderment at all turns. The game doesn't hand hold you and you are generally free to explore and discover yourself, which is rare in most games. Its always a surprise when you discover a little sound bit, or photo that suddenly evokes a memory or feeling.

A real no-brainer to recommend anyone who likes adventure, exploration and a deep dive soul searching game.

I simply want more of this world.

review_text_for_llm:
In short, a game about what you choose to remember and how.

You've got a camera, a tape recorder, and a journal. The game has you essentially scrapbook your way through your journey where you can choose what you want to take pictures of and record and sketch and you can race all the way to the "End" of the game.

That said, there's significant detail in the world that you might find yourself taking more pictures than you can fit in the book, or recording sounds that aren't all that significant. 

The world isn't particularly large, but it is gorgeous to look at, and there's a surprising amount of things to see in my opinion.
Something looks interesting? Take a picture of it, or record how it sounds. There's a significant level of inner dialog about mundane things from a new perspective. It's just up to you to decide what's important.

I probably spent more time biking around in this game than I needed to finish it, but most all of that additional time was just taken slowly to stop and smell the roses along the way.

Ultimately it's up to you to decide what's important enough to carry on to the future; and you can't stop the future from coming

It's not a huge game (took me around 11 hours to finish it), but that's exactly the amount of playtime i expect from games like this. A bit longer would have been nice, but not much longer.

Only thing i didn't like: There are some weird performance issues. Overall the game was running good at 80+ fps without any framerate limiter, but for some reason this game put huge amounts of load on my GPU (RTX 2080, game running at 1440p). To avoid that i tried to limit the framerate. First to 72, then to 60, then 48... didn't help much. Even at 48 fps the game sometimes puts 99% load on my GPU and after a while it starts overheating. The last sections of the game i limited the framerate to 30 fps (doesn't look nor feel good) to avoid overheating my gpu. Hrot is a game I really, really wanted to like, but feel really short for me. I get the "everything is brown" color scheme is meant to evoke Soviet brutalism, and it does that really well, but it makes for incredibly boring and unengaging levels. The game's tone is very mellow and flat, and while there are elements of horror in it, things like a pommel horse coming to life and firing rockets at you is too silly for the tone the game establishes. All of that can be forgiven, but the game commits the cardinal sin of FPS: The guns just suck. Very little hit feedback, really weak sound effects, and very little animation to convey power.

Hrot is absolutely admirable for it's scope and development, but ultimately it ends up being an unenjoyable experience.

review_text_for_llm:
Hrot is drugs.

Ok but in all seriousness...

Truth be told, this is a game I can see underwhelming a lot of people.
It is effectively a cocktail of random ideas that are all loosely Slavic-ly
themed. These are then smashed together into a retro shooter experience that whilst it
has a lot of charm and personality doesn't seem to have a very singular
vision in terms of what it wants to be.

It is effectively the haunted house of retro shooters.
You hop from level to level on a sightseeing tour as the
game plays with quirky little gimmicks. The combat feel
endearingly dinky and is very shallow. The level design
is okay, and there's not really much else to the experience.

It is a fun and charming time, one I'd say you should
at least give a try. But I wouldn't be shocked if it didn't wow ya.

+ Cool atmosphere
+ Motorcycle
+ Interactive world a la Duke Nukem 3D (you can turn stuff on/off etc)
++ Great level design.
++ Good controls

- Most of the enemy projectiles looks the same. For me it lessens the weird creepy atmosphere and makes the arcade-game vibe stronger. 
- One of the achievements is a mini game that has nothing to do with the rest of the game. It's entirely optional but if you want to 100% the game you need to slog through it.. Very boring and not a creative way to use achievements. 
-- Everything is the color brown all the time. This aesthetic without an equalizer becomes a bit uninspiring after a while.
-- The sound effects are very thin and the weapon audio sounds like it's coming from toys. I would prefer punchier and rawer sound effects (Chasm: The Rift is a master of this)

I'd say it's a 7/10. It's enjoyable for fans of old school FPS games, but doesn't offer much. The action and guns are ok. The music design is great; all except for the sound effects for the weapons. Almost all the guns have no oomph or bass to the sound, so they all sound like pea shooters and it really detracts from the experience. It's one of those things where you're so used to things sounding good in other games that when it's missing you really notice it. Something else that's odd to me is that this game seems a bit confused about it's identity. It has a really creepy vibe and sound to it, there are even jump scares, but there's also a lot of weird comedy that seems out of place to me. I dunno maybe it's just me. In particular that final level just had me scratching my head. It's also very short, I finished it in about 7 hours.

Overall I'd recommend this game on a sale; maybe I just don't get the hype but if you're looking for an old school shooter and haven't played Dusk, Amid Evil, or Ion Fury yet then I'd recommend those over this.

Calling HROT "Quake but Soviet" is selling it short. It's so smooth. The level design and atmosphere are so good. This is the type of retro FPS that should be supported and celebrated.
Funny how another certain retro shooter (one that shall not be named) went into early access 4 years ago, 2 years before HROT. It charged more than HROT, and offered less. That game is still not out and has seen no updates in years unless you get excited seeing biweekly dev updates showcasing those epic upcoming new vase textures whoop-de-doo! (Yeah, you know which game it is. Well done.)

Why was all this relevant? Because on the other side of early access... you have good developers who know what they're doing like Gloomwood's, DUSK's, and of course... [b]HROT's[/b]. (Presumably) One gigathad fueled by nothing but actual player feedback and vodka, pumping out  improvements and level after level on a consistent basis throughout 28 months of early access. 
When people point to the aforementioned poopy game as a reason why you should never get games in Early Access, HROT is one of the few that prove the opposite by simply saying "Actually, yes it can work".

Good on you, Spytihněv. Vashe zdorov'ye.

Hrot is a superb, brown game. It's a lot of fun to just tear around in, ripping and tearing, and if the obvious Quake inspiration is all you need to get circlestrafing then you won't be disappointed. The levels are fun, the enemies varied enough to keep the gameplay fresh with new combinations and the movement and shooting feel good. There's also an excellent sense of humour to the whole enterprise that revels in a very Czech-style dry wit combined with joyful surrealism. The episode bosses in particular are a real weird highlight and the final level peaks in the gag department in a series of superb bait-and-switch ploys that I won't spoil. An easy recommend just on the surface level.
Going a little deeper, there're some very well-hidden secrets that can become fun to hunt down once you get a flavour of them and what to look for. There are also lots of achievements for odd behaviours and quirky little things unique to each level; having them pop up unexpectedly is a nice surprise and you can have more fun guessing what might trigger them.

Made by a single developer it takes you on a monochromatic journey through Czechoslovakia where an "unspecified" disaster populated the area with hostiles, including flying Lenin heads and horses with gasmasks. If you've played any other game like that then you know what to expect. Neatly designed levels inspired by the classics, lots of secrets, lots of shooting and blowing things up, end-level stats and toilets. Ultimately, if you think the premise sounds cute and you want something that's very visually distinct from other puzzle roguelikes, you should give this a shot. If you're looking for a million hours of content and a high base difficulty, there may be other games that better fit your bill.

[h1]An interactive painting[/h1]

Unleaving describes itself modestly as "Limbo, with a splash of color" and that is quite an apt way of thinking of this gem. Throughout this ~3 hour experience, you will be delighted by its art, music, and clever gameplay.
Please, immerse yourself...

Cinematic platformers are a rarity, and one such as this one is completely unique even among its tiny niche. Along the game while traveling forward, you'll be faced with simple platforming challenges and quite a bit more not-so-simple puzzles. You will feel like a genius for solving them, but they're never so difficult to make you completely stuck. There is also a hint system in place in case you need a nudge in the right direction. Controls are snappy, animations are fluid, challenges are greatly varied.

The world around you moves, as if always in motion. Everything is hand painted, and it shows: it's one of the most beautiful games in recent memory.

[h3]Pros:[/h3]
[list]
    [*]Gorgeous, looks and sounds amazing
    [*]Tight controls
    [*]Mind bending puzzles
    [*]Emotional journey
    [*]Priced appropriately
[/list]

Having played this on early access and found it to be just ok, I have to give it up to the developers for making huge improvements to the finished product and making a pretty dang solid action platformer that feels reminiscent of the late PS2/early PS3 era, with a few caveats. 

Pros:

+Combat flows well
+There's a really nice variety of skills
+The maps are big enough that they're pretty enjoyable to go through and there's enough in them to make exploration worthwhile
+The puzzles feel challenging without being too frustrating.
+The game genuinely looks great for what it is
 
Cons:

-Targetting with the slingshot feels very finicky at times
-Our sidekick, Piggy, feels more annoying then helpful most of the time
-The map could use some work, especially while using a controller. 
-Story overall is fine and serviceable but the dialogue can be a little clunky at times

Overall a pretty enjoyable experience despite the cons and one that I can see becoming even better with just a few fixes.

7.5/10

Simple fun, has local co-op, all cosmetics in game. It's not going to blow your mind, but its a great reminder that games that focus on fun will always be classic. If you enjoy just exploring maps with a buddy and laughing at all the mayhem, you'll love this game. Every corner of the map seems to have some stuff to do, and co-op was pretty seamless (until it crashed, but progress was saved so no issues there.) The controls and general gameplay are simple, but the maps are designed to make the most of your physics interactions and get you to explore different areas. From just the first map, I can tell this is going to be a fun time for local co-op.

Steam Controller (and by extension Steam Deck) also feels great with this game. I just used whatever default config was, and the controls were great. Touchpad camera controls feels natural, even better than stick. Only gripe so far is that local co-op camera can feel a little zoomed in since you're already sharing half the screen with someone, and some options menus are cropped when in local co-op split screen. Could probably be solved with camera options to avoid zoom in and keep it locked to certain distances when possible.

I used the standard coop mode and the mode for two separate monitors in the nvidia panel. The camera in two was hopeless. Every now and then it would block, hide behind vegetation and it was hard to navigate anything. In my opinion, releasing the game in version 1.0 should be fixed, lack of legibility in some situations, what to do and where to go and not very sharp graphics, I felt like I was playing games from the PS3 era. Personally for me the map and more information was missing. The second problem for me is (I haven't watched any game footage or read) very poorly explained aspects of items. Acquiring a sword in Viking land, I wanted to use it, but couldn't figure out how. It was natural for me to be able to use it, but I didn't (I guess.) There was no notification of what to do with it or how to do it. Playing 1.5h with my girlfriend we were tired of the game and so I decided to refund. It's not a game for us, unfortunately, which is a shame because I liked the idea and a lot of the content at the initial stage.

Regardless, I had a lot of fun with it, and I definitely recommend it if you like 3D open-zone platformers!

review_text_for_llm: I really dig "Children of the Sun". You play a masked sniper - whose look reminded me somewhat of the movie "The Crow" - on a mission to wipe out some kind of religious group. The details are hazy, as the plot is presented through a bunch of confusing cartoons. That's fine though. We've learned from "Hotline Miami" that context is not a necessary pre-requisite, but a seasoning. "Children of the Sun", unlike "Hotline Miami" is not a franticly-paced action game. It's a strange kind of puzzle piece, where you guide one single bullet from enemy to enemy, sometimes bending time and space to land a perfect head shot. Through a liberal use of slow motion, it gives you ample time to consider your next move. The catch is that you have to nail all the enemies with one bullet, and the bullet can't touch anything that doesn't bleed or explode, or it's game over. Is that sort of ridiculous? Oh yes. Is it great gameplay? Duh! "Children of the Sun" does its premise justice, and fully delivers on the potential of its central gimmick. Its grungy aesthetics, noise-filled soundtrack and ridiculously violent gameplay hit just the right spot for me.

review_text_for_llm:
Children of the Sun is a puzzle shooter stripped down to just the core puzzles and the aesthetic. The style is very minimalist and psychedelic, the plot is barely there and follows the jumbled chronology of your protagonist's crumbling mind, the levels themselves contain lots of "errors" that quickly become too obvious and drastic to be anything but either magical or psychosis on the part of the protagonist.

And it works! The puzzles are what's on display here and they're good. Everything else works towards communicating how broken the protagonist is. The puzzles are truly unique and very satisfying... and the plot communicates a story about how our need for control damages the people around us. There's so little here but everything works because they put the thought into making sure it was put together excellently.

And the price! It's so cheap! Well worth the cost of entry. If you want shorter games with worse graphics made by people who are paid more to work less and you're not kidding... this is a game for you.

First things first: There is a demo, and although it is enjoyable, it pales in comparison to the released game.

This is a solid and enjoyable roguelite. If you know and like the genre, then this a "one more run" type of game. I really think this is a hidden gem that is flying under the radar. The controls take a little getting used to, but are fun when you start strafing in a circle around your target and focusing fire. FTL meets Asteroids meets No Man's Sky (sorta).

The negative reviews don't seem to understand how a rogulite gameloop works. The game is about rinse and repeat, with upgrades in between runs. One review mentions ammo scarcity, which to me is fine as a resource managing mechanic from the start. However, I think after 2-3 runs is when I started getting the max ammo upgrades. Another review mentions just boring gaps in flying through space. I don't think they experienced their ship rocketing across a map after using the warp gates.

The game will not hold your hand, but it has a tutorial that serves its purpose. The fun of a roguelite, at least to me, is getting right into the action and discovering new things through trial and error.

What made Farewell North special to me, and something that I wanted to highlight is that it joins the collective of games with positive Scottish representation, and is probably my favourite example in anything I've played. It was always is a nice surprise for things like munros and Hogmanay in Edinburgh to be referenced, and I thought the exploration of cultural erasure and feeling compelled to modify aspects of yourself to make your identity more palatable e.g [spoiler] Cèilidh reclaiming her original spelling of her name as she reconnects with her Mum and where she came from [/spoiler], was a really great inclusion.

I love story games that can make me cry and Farewell North had me in tears basically from beginning to end - it's really clear that the developers cared a lot about this project and absolutely poured everything they had into it, with stellar results. Would recommend to fans of story games and dog lovers everywhere!

I could say a lot about this game.
This game is beautiful, and has a wonderful fitting score and a story with wonderful pacing and depth.
This game may not be for everyone, but a lot of people will enjoy it and some may shed a few tears in the process.

There is a lot to explore here and a lot of interactive gameplay, some light puzzles, and a few funny stories.
The different islands and skerries you will explore are unique and some are really memorable. There are at least 12 hours of unique gameplay to do. Doing 100% in this game is a lot of fun and easy to do, even in post main game. Thinking about it, this is more of an interactive experience than a game you play when you are bored, this is an art piece.

Also, the community behind this game and all the wonderful pet pictures that got shared are amazing. The bond between you as the pet and your human and the exploration of that is something a lot of people can relate to.

Overall I think this game is a must-play, so stop reading and buy or wishlist the game!
I promise, that if this game gives you good vibes, you will enjoy it.

At first I had a bit of trouble with the canoe rowing system but quickly enough got the hang out of it! 
Another thing I would like to point out is that the score is top notch and goes hand in hand with the atmospheric Scottish landscape and vibes the game coveys towards the player (I was already in love with the music the first time I heard "My Heart's in the Highlands" in one of the trailers and I was happy to see that the song is actually part of a side quest!).

Alltogether I can recommend this game to everybody who is looking for a lovely story-driven, relaxing and emotional adventure with the occasional puzzle-elements!

Ultimate Chicken Horse meets Mashed: Fully Loaded and Micro Machines.

This game manages to capture the gameplay of Mashed/Micro Machines very well to the point it is almost nostalgic.Even the items are very close to what Micro Machines V4 had. The twist here is you and other players are building the course instead.

You want to sabotage your friends by putting a boost pad on a sharp corner? Go ahead. Want to make a gauntlet of crushers? Also possible. The best part of this game is the players are responsible for whatever monstrosity of a course they come up with.  

I would recommend playing this game with friends for the best chaotic experience, but the offline bots also provide a bit of challenge on the harder difficulty.

You have to unlock vehicles and those funny track pieces through playing the game, but a huge chunk of the starter pieces are already available so you don't feel too limited when starting out.

Overall. definitely recommended if you're looking for something to fill the micro-machine shaped hole in your heart.

Excellent party game! 

Love the micro machines/ultimate chicken horse cross over. Played locally and remotely, 2, 3 and 4 players, worked with no issues. Even with couple of randoms joining in, even with out emotes or communication with the new players, the friendly  competitive edge was still there, it was great fun. But i agree with the previous review, emotes would be an ideal addition to a least have friendly banter, congratulations and thanking for a good game.

And it's addictive, unlocking new section of track and traps, which are all well designed and interesting, help make you come back for more. Even if with everything unlocked, I feel it will still have replay value and just like ultimate chicken horse it will be a staple for our Steam Games Night. 

I like the simple controls and it feel smooth for the most part it can be a bit 'janky' at times but think that add to the enjoyment of the game. It's not a 'serious' game, it's fun, ridiculous and chaotic, especially the aptly named Chaos level, which is just nuts. 

I'll definitely be recommending this to all.

Cheers guys! <3

With colorful and creative characters and a difficult but satisfying combat system, Punch A Bunch is a blast to play. It can be frustratingly difficult at times, as it's brutal bosses demand a precision that it's physics based combat doesn't always allow; but it's that same system that allows for combat that actually feels like real boxing. You can dodge and weave through your opponents volley of blows, keep outside their range and punish when they over extend, push in close to get inside their guard to deny their heaviest hits, or block blow after blow until they're out of stamina and then turn the tables with your own series of haymakers. Eventually you'll find yourself wiping the floor with the fighters that gave you the most trouble in the early game. 

I'd recommend this game to anyone who thought that Dark Souls was fun, but that it would have been better if it was more of a slapstick comedy.

The real highlight for me is the hacking, which allows you to type commands to open doors, control enemies, spy remote locations, and so much more. My great-aunt was just over 20 years old when the Germans took her to a labor camp. She was able to return home by walking across the country. It was an incredibly difficult path, full of dangers and hardships. She faced hunger, cold and fatigue, but none of these challenges compared to the fear she carried inside herself. Her soul was riddled with painful memories of the cruelty and loss she experienced in the camp. But despite all this, she did not tell anyone about her past. None of her loved ones and relatives knew what happened to her in those terrible days.

My great-aunt was a woman with a huge heart. She didn't have her own family, but she found family in other people's children and grandchildren. She gave them all her love, care and support. My dad still remembers her care and tenderness with warmth. Her life was full of sacrifice and dedication, and she did everything she could to make the lives of others better.

I want to thank the creators of the game for Asya’s story. This game evokes a lot of emotions and feelings in me. It shows that war is not only death and destruction, but also fear, loss, loneliness. It makes you think about how war affects people, their future

review_text_for_llm:
An excellent game that will break your heart when you realize it is telling a story that happens to civilians all over the world, in all time periods. To sum it up... war is hell.

You play as a young Russian girl (Aysa) who gets caught in the crossfire of WW2 as the Germans battle in Russia. Your life as a child is forever altered by the wartime experience and the developers did a great job of capturing the collateral damage of war. They made you feel as if you are in the middle of a conflict, even though the game has no graphic violence or bloody scenes. 

Torn Away is part point-and-click and part side-scroller. There are calm scenes with small tasks, stealth scenes that require observation and timing, and survival scenes that require evasion and speed. The penalty for failure is to restart the failed sequence. I was okay with the stealth scenes but the timed jumps and gunfire evasion took me quite a few tries to get through. Your progress is auto-saved on a fairly regular basis and at the end of each chapter. It is not saved on exit so you need to be careful if you are inclined to quit in the middle of a tough section.  Once you complete the game, you can return to any chapter

review_text_for_llm:
A nice, relaxing game that's focused solely on mining - nice variety of resources, attention to detail, a pleasant thing to decompress after work. Co-op included so you can drill some dirt with your buddies. If you liked Motherlode you should get it. If you liked Steamworld Dig but were annoyed by the monsters - the same.

There are various mechs you can upgrade (sadly no visual customisation), multiple player characters to pick from and humorous dialogues.

The game supports atypical ultrawide resolutions out of the box (21:9 and 32:9) - no hacks / ini edit needed. 

For me personally the music doesn't really fit the game but it isn't bad - but I like to listen to podcasts playing such games anyway so overall it's not relevant.

Additional huge plus: the dev is very responsive - fixes bugs and improves stuff very fast.

And to sum it up - the game is also priced very well (worth the full price too!) - especially for amount of fun it brings. It's an example why indie games are the future of this type of entertainment (not cash-grabby, unoptimized and greedy AAA games). Support good devs and nice games, get this one :)

So Im gonna give this a positive review simply because there's very few entries in the genre and the price is cheap, but I might switch to a negative later on.

For people who want a relaxing experience this game will fit your needs. There is no failure, no combat and the only "bad" choice you can make is to not dig left or right missing out on some ores. However since you can dig from the top at any tile this means you can't really mess up.

The biggest negative against this game is its writing. It feels too amatuerish. Lines feel random, and while humour is subjective, there's no group I feel like that will think it's funny. I'm someone who grew up on random humour (millenial) and zoomer humour can be quite random at times too, but this ain't it. Dialogue in video games like these are supposed to be fun, rewarding or world building. You should look forward to getting the next piece of dialogue. Here I just cringe.

Oh yeah and the artstyle is all over the place. Some extremely low bit sprites mixed with higher bit sprites generally never looks good.

Give it a shot, you'll not regret it.

So this is a pretty nice roguelite deckbuilder concept, and if you don't mind the low playtime it's worth the price.

But the thing is, I've already beaten it and feel like i've seen everything it has to offer, which is a bit underwhelming considering it took me about four attempts - compared to other similar roguelite deckbuilders this just isn't enough content imo. Especially since I didn't actually unlock many new parts until my winning run - it feels like there ought to be some progression, a second stage or a hardmode.
It needs some kind of run modifier variants and more enemies at the very least, as well as maybe some variant battle objectives beyond 'kill everything' - it is supposed to be 'racing' after all.

Another issue is a lot of the parts you have access to just feel underwhelming and too similar. A LOT of the power here comes from passive stat boosts attached to parts rather than the cards they give you - stacking armour is very important if you want to make it far into the game, as healing can be sparse and having a ~30+ HP buffer is incredibly useful.

As a Car Wars player from the olden days I really enjoyed this. At first glance it doesn't seem to have much depth but as you level up, you unlock new "parts" which make runs easier.
There are a lot of negative comments on difficulty & health, but this is a strategic game and not a shooter. If you're facing 4 enemies, you're going to get splattered if you can't figure out a way to mitigate their actions. Reducing their handling (so they can't play cards), putting distance between you and some of them, or even simply escaping the fights you can't win, are all viable options. I've just finished the game and it wasn't too difficult. Armour is super important as it regens every fight, so stacking armour rather than health is a much better option. Weapons that deliver DoT, and cards that increase your damage (rage/overload) will have you beating the game in no time.
Well worth a tenner. Got my £1/hour out of it that's for sure.

It was really interesting how much this feels like the first game even though there is a new style to it, as I just finished playing the first game when I started this. Either way this is a fun Zelda like adventure game that I enjoyed quite a bit. 

My biggest issue was just with exploration and a tracking of events, the stamina bar empties quite quickly while running around and it can take quite a bit of time to cover ground, you do get more as you level but even towards the end it felt sluggish having to slow down to let it recharge often.

As for tracking there is a good feature of showing you whats in each individual zone and they blink near the radar when you are looking in the direction it's in, but it gets worse with for example in a village the tracking only shows outside it doesn't include what's in each building which has it's own independent tracking for it's own items and there are some fairly well hidden areas that were hard to find, so going for the 100% zone completion can be a little hard for some zones as you might not know where exactly the missing items are.

review_text_for_llm:
I almost hate to give this a "no" because there's nothing terrible about this game. It's actually quite polished and it does deliver a game.

It's just that, rather than anything being BAD about the game, nothing is particularly GOOD. Everything from the graphics to the combat to the puzzles and world design feels like it's just "good enough to be a game". This would be fine if there were one or two things the game excels at, but it really excels at nothing.

The game has this weird "default Unity mechanics" vibe with its mechanics, like what you'd see in one of those clickbait videos like "I remade Simpsons Hit & Run in Unity". Sure, they WORK fine, but they feel very uninspired. That said, I don't want to give the impression that this is an asset flip or something. It's an actual game with actual original art and content, and the music is pretty decent too.

If you're REALLY clamoring for a Zelda-like, particularly older 3D Zelda titles, this might be fun, though don't get your hopes up thinking that this is nearly as good as those games are.

So, limitations of boomer-shooter father Wolfenstein 3D: no verticality, no jump, maze-like levels. What do I get in return?

Technically, there are some mechanical complexity:
1. More weapons each with secondary fire? Ok. Some of them are not bad, but gunplay is lacking.
2. Consumables? Meh. Neither practical, nor interesting. Not fun to use.
3. Spells? Meh. The game can live without them just fine.
4. Weapon shop? Meh. Not fun, not many choices. It is just there for the sake of it.
5. Visual verticality? Good, it makes some areas on the levels more memorable. Also, it makes you wonder why you are not allowed to drop from the ledge. This is undestandable design desicion, but it just not pleasant one.
6. Interesting combat? No. Enemies are dumb and not that numerous.

I really wanted to like Wizordum. It has a lot of charm to it, with a good retro artstyle and decent magic combat.

But it's bland, oh so bland. It's slower paced than a snail caught in a glue trap. The levels are massive and labyrinthine with enemy counts in the hundreds, but most of the time you'll only be fighting 2-3 enemies per room. You'll likely spend more time exploring, breaking barrels and opening chests than actually fighting.

Most of the enemies are not very engaging to fight. You got your standard roster of melee and ranged foes you'll be fighting in mostly square rooms or long corridors. The AI is very basic, making most encounters feel very samey. The level design, while visually appealing, also suffers from having a lot of samey looking areas. Once you've beaten a couple levels, you'll have seen most of what the game has to offer.

It took me 6 hours to beat the first chapter and the game was already feeling like a chore at that point so I couldn't bring myself to finish it.  In terms of mechanics and combat it's a perfectly okay game, but I can only really recommend it to people with a high tolerance for repetition.

It plays like most "sim" games and has a fun level of progression and in its current state feels more like a Early Access title. I haven't had any technical issues and have been enjoying this clever take on base building. The 360 degree jetpack exploration, combat and spaceship construction is an entertaining genre twist that really has to be experienced first hand to full appreciate. The variable directional gravity challenges you to come up with new efficiency planning and ergonomic paradigms. For example, I was building my initial factory layout and realized that, instead of the typical 2D plane approach, placing them like spokes around the hub of a wheel was actually more efficient. Then figuring out how to do that and make it feel intuitive an accessible is an enjoyable challenge. 

I also love the chill music and the way you jetpack around to explore little worlds and derelicts, or over to wreckage to carve it up with your mining laser. Given how low the price of entry is for this game, if you are any kind of fan of base building and looking for a new challenge you should give Space Trash Scavengers a try.

Space Trash Scavenger drops you into a procedurally-generated system where you must loot the varied asteroids and derelict freighters to find the materials to survive in this curious sector of the cosmos.

The core loop is scavenge, atomise, build, upgrade, scavenge more, repeat. Building up your Space-rig is super satisfying once your platform is bristling with turrets and reinforced walls. Combat comes in the form of the Entity who will be guarding most of the good wreck sites and will mount retaliation attacks on your rig.

STS isn't a hardcore factory game but the materials and elements all make sense and it has some very satisfying production chains that will net you the big bucks from ScavCorp. STS is a super charming space adventure with a great soundtrack that you can see and feel the love the devs have put into it. Recommended.

It feels like a throwback to old school boardsport games, with real surfers and licensed music and gear. You can create a custom surfer and unlock/buy boards, wetsuits, jet skis, and skill points, giving the game an RPG element.
Graphically, the game is pretty unimpressive. You won't really notice this once you're riding waves though. Generally, you're scored for your best two runs (i.e. waves), and can take on as many waves as you want within a time limit. You can't just rack up points; you have to make one or two decent runs to compete with the AI surfing alongside you. This makes each run tense, as you gain combos and rack up points while avoiding whipeouts.
There's a decent tutorial, and a Freesurf mode that lets you practice in customizable conditions and explore the dozen or so locations at your leisure, which is super relaxing.

review_text_for_llm: Looking for an ethereal retro fps gem? There's a lot of charm to the system in Soul King. The characters are well thought out with their own personalities adding uniqueness to each dreamscape. The hub space pulls this experience together. It's one of those games where I'll say "I'll just play one more" and then proceed to play three more. Most of my deaths were just from instinctively holding Shift + W or relying too much on strafing rather than aiming. While sprinting you cannot switch weapons. Which makes sense, but it might feel more satisfying to have weapon switches act as a sprint cancel. I wish most weapon reloads were just half a second faster, but that's largely from my struggle to master the system at work here. How, when, and why you switch to a weapon is how you'll improve each stage. There's good inventory management to unlock and pick a loadout that suits your play style. In game leader board is very nice and there's a small enough player base that you could actually work to get a top score! I was very impressed with how well the aesthetics of its art, story, and system worked together in this game. Had a lot of fun with Soul King!

Good language/cryptography based logic game, with an emphasis on exploring a visually striking world.  The puzzles themselves are fairly easy and straightforward, but still satisfying when everything clicks into place.  I would have liked more opportunities to test my mastery of the different languages as that was the most enjoyable part of the puzzle solving; your understanding is never pushed very far, even when reaching the climax and final sections of the game. Chants of Sennaar is a bit less complex mechanics-wise than others in this logic puzzler niche but makes up for it in world building, the tower is an enchanting place with interesting secrets to uncover until the very end.  Traversal mechanics can be a little clunky but it was nothing more than a minor annoyance.  
 
8.5/10, recommend if you enjoy Return of the Obra Dinn and other games in this genre and don't mind a slightly easier experience, or if you're at all intrigued by the tower of babelesque setting.

To me it looks like a love child of Journey and Heaven's Gate - linguistics, exploration and simplicity.

Pros:
+ Beautiful
+ Cool linguistic puzzles
+ Fleshed-out factions
+ The soundtrack matches the story beats nicely.

Cons:
- Puzzles can be bruteforced (It took me a while to understand how the notebook works)
- The gameplay and story drops-off at the last stage. It's not bad per-se but it's worse (imo) than the first two stages. The end sequence even more so.

Oh boy, I'm torn on this. Chants of Sennaar was recommended to me as a slow-paced language translation game, and the first level absolutely excels at that.

And then the second level rolls in, and now it's a stealth game requiring exact timing and precision movement.

I tried really hard, I swear. I tried. But the number of times the game pulled me out of cover because it thought I clicked somewhere I didn't -- the number of times I ran out of cover because I didn't know an NPC could see me -- the number of times I tried, over and over, to get through this one bloody arena... and it just isn't worth the frustration.

The first level is full of some of the smartest language puzzles I've ever played, but the game seems as ashamed as it is proud. The constant pop-ups telling you what you press are patronising. Before I got used to the slow and uninterruptible animations, I thought someone was wrong. The lack of responsiveness isn't a deal-breaker for language puzzle games, but throw in the raging stealth and it just ain't worth it.

I wish I loved it as much as the rest of you are.

A Grindy and Unrewarding Arcade game.
Weapons inflict very little damage and are very unprecise. So, shooting in this game is all about tanking more damage than your enemy.
You get weapons after completing missions, which would be good if it rewarded you with a weapon related to the class you chose to play that mission, but instead you get a lootbox that rolls for a random weapon. So if you want something that fits your playstyle, repeat the mission (or play other ones) until you get something you like.
Also, weapons have rarities and levels, which I may be biased to hate from other games. (It usually means more grind)
Abilities are locked behind levels, which rewards "time spent playing" and not skill.
I wanted to try out the multiplayer, but without a solid gameplay loop in singleplayer, I lost interest before getting to the multiplayer content.

This game may work better for you if you play it with a casual mindset. It didn't work for me.

You play as a warden and your job is to collect Ambrosia each night while avoiding the Devourer who contaminates it. Gather enough Ambrosia to survive the season. There are five nights per season and each season has you play as a different character with their own backstory and a starting trait. I really don't like posting negative reviews. Especially when it's so obvious that someone has put their heart and soul into a project. But I also need to be honest. And my honest belief is that most people won't enjoy this game. 

The first few hours were fun. I liked the physics and the track design felt perfectly in tune with that. But once I got to BTCC S2000 and DTM cars, that enjoyment evaporated. The tracks they get are boring, often flat out with few interesting corners or braking zones. And the touring cars feel leaden to drive, somehow much less agile or lively than the rustbuckets from the first hour. 

It's a particularly painful as the vast majority of the game revolves around these two categories. They're not only the reward you're tantalised with for the first few hours, they're most of the game. For them to be so uninspiring, even >boring< to drive is difficult to overlook. And for me, removed any enjoyment or motivation to continue.

3/10.

What an awesome little game this is. Loads of content from normal stock car racing to timed rally tracks as well as an awesome community feature where you get to race specific races that change every week and you get ranked compared to everyone else that takes part in those races. This game is clearly a labour of love to old school retro arcade top-down racers such as neo drift out. It even has an arcade mode that tries to mimic the feeling of old arcades. The game supports a few video options that try to emulate old crt tvs but I felt the curvature was a bit strong for my taste and I've enjoyed playing with curved shaders on retroarch. I'd appreciate a standard shader with just the basic crt lines going across but unfortunately this game doesn't appear to contain that. the controls are also good but I'm let down by the exclusion of the d-pad for turning. The tracks so far also seem really cool and inventive. 
all in all, so far i'd give this game a 9/10 but I haven't really done a lot yet. This might change in the future.

Fantastic game. Tons of cars to buy/unlock/upgrade. Several game modes. A lot of different tracks. Tight game play. 

Really, I haven't had that much fun with a racing game in a while. Everything just feels right. The game is not easy, but things never feel cheap or unfair. It's so satisfying to win once you master a track, getting that perfect lap. It's quite addictive and the game manages to keep you coming back for more even when you lose 10 times in a row.

Tracks are unlocked via Stars that you obtain when winning first place, and as such, it takes some effort to unlock races. But progression seems fairly organic. I'm not great at these games, and even for me the learning curve feels fine. Though I can only imagine how tough the later races must be!

All the cars I've tried were super fun to drive and really felt unique as well. So MANY cars! It's awesome!

It also looks as though ViJuDa will put in some regular updates with new cars/tracks/races so that's cool too.

Anyway, this game is a steal. Absolutely worth it. Get it.

[h3] A Return to Greatness [/h3]
      Super Woden GP 2 is a easy to pick up and hard to master arcade racer that has me hooked, since buying the game I haven't been able to put it down! The vast selection of cars remind me of the idols that graced the raceways, magazine covers and streets that I grew up with, also being able to change the art style on the fly with many different choices such as the pencil style lets you relive the feel of games such as Auto Modellista or the pixel style similar to World Rally '93.
      I've read other people liken the story mode to that of the golden age of racing games king that was Gran Turismo and it couldn't be closer,leven little details and animations like changing oil and washing your cars appear to add to the likeness. The varying classes and events allow you to experience every avenue of racing from sub 80hp french vans to 900hp oval racers, Group B icons, British touring car and beyond! 
      Overall if you want to enjoy a single player racer full of polish and climb your way up the online leader boards so everyone sees your name you can't go wrong with this game!

This game is not a very good detective game. First, I should point the superficial flaws: The game is extremely buggy. Every other time I opened the journal (something that is necessary very often), I ran into either a game-crash or a softlock, which required me to restart the program. To the game's credit, I should point out that it autosaves constantly and I did not have to replay any segments due to this. But even so, having to go back through all the start menus about once every hour is not an ideal gameplay experience.

Another superficial flaw is that the game is difficult to read. The text stored in the journal is of a font that is thin enough such that some pieces of the letters do not show up at all at the game's default resolution. In addition, the size of the text characters and spacing of the letters makes it difficult to read the text at a glance. The testimonies cannot be zoomed in on at all, and some of the documents' text was still illegible even when viewed at full zoom. Having completed the game and gotten both endings, I feel like I'm in a better position to explain my feelings about this game, so I've decided to update my review.

I don't have much to say about the gameplay. But, though I would generally agree that it's better than the first, I do have a few complaints: The new weapons are a gimmick. There was only one boss fight in which I found myself switching between weapons. It would've been better to either force the player to use only one of the weapons throughout the game (thus locking them to a certain play style), or to have a singular weapon that we could equip different skills to. Alas, these weapons turned out to be little more than glorified relics. 
That's not all. Thanks to these things, blocking as a game mechanic, while still there, has become rather unintuitive to the point I almost never used it. Fortunately (unfortunately), outside of a few boss fights, you don't need to block either: enemies have been declawed and most of your battles consist of being swarmed by them rather than focusing on a few, dangerous ones. You'll spend most of your time dodging instead. Overall it feels like combat has been dumbed down, not improved.

Stone Age, the physical board game, has been a family favourite. The digital version captures it really well. The tutorial was OK, although I did not see anything explaining the cards, which for someone new to the game would make it hard to grasp first off. Gameplay is smooth, and I have had no significant glitches, although I have only played solo against the AI. As others have said, that can be a pretty testing challenge, even at the Easy AI level. It will take a good grasp of the game and sound basic tactics to beat even the Easy AI. Ideally, as is the case with Through the Ages, there would be a learner level, which really makes it easier for new users to learn the game and get their first victories. I saw a reviewer complaining about the need to confirm moves. I disagree. In my view, this is necessary, and once you have played a few times, this really does not add much extra time to the game. 

All in all, it's a great port, and I would highly recommend it to fans of Stone Age, as well as others who have not played the hard copy of the board game.

Interesting horror game. I liked the graphics and art style, the jump scares in the beginning were decent, and its probably an ok price, even though its a rather short game (under 2 hours). I had a gamebreaking bug in the beginning, but that has been fixed overnight, and I have since completed the game. 

If I had some criticism its that there are lots of the same assets copy pasted all over the place (there isn't much locker variety for instance). The game surely wouldn't have suffered from more variety.

Theres not anything resembling a real puzzle, in my opinion. And trust me, I solved a fair share of puzzles in all the horror games I play. Maybe that could be improved on for the next game. So far its mostly find key-open door, with just a little variety on where the key is. 

I feel that the first part of the game was more atmospheric, while the latter part consists of looking for a key while Ghost Lady looks for YOU.

If you want to check the gameplay for yourself, or maybe just enjoy watching Horror Let's Plays where I don't take most things too seriously, look no further: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FwQMNcs7kfE

review_text_for_llm:
I don't recommend this for anyone who isn't the introspective sort. If you are then this is a very nice thought provoker. There is a lot to think about the questions you ask, even if you only ever have two options.

The only thing I didn't like that I can think of is the "hidden 3rd fate". I got the Redemption ending for Markus, a judgement I was satisfied with, given the body of evidence available. The Fateweaver's policy of "thumbs up or thumbs down" works well because it's binary: either you're doing well, or you need to taste dirt. However, the moment you introduce nuance, it becomes a hamfisted approach, and third options always mean nuance, and with nuance comes a vast array of perspectives that contribute to how a decision is made and carried out. Additionally, while the game tells you that there is no wrong choice, that is only true in the sense that there is no external source of authority who makes that judgement; except there is a wrong choice relative to my own judgement. With a 3rd option and nuance introduced, to me it feels like the game steers away from essentially being an introspection prompt and toward a godlike detective game, except I can't ask all the question

"He writes 'em to play 'em."
is displayed in black as you open the game. A tagline from an old ad, but it slowly dawns on you that this is the thesis of Llamasoft: The Jeff Minter Story.
The second of the Gold Master series from Digital Eclipse that are less retro game collection and more digital museum exhibit, Llamasoft: The Jeff Minter Story invites you into a comprehensive of the first twenty years of Jeff Minter's career and encourages you to treat as indeed the exhibit of an artist. Just like any other artist exhibit, you slowly see Jeff grow in technical proficiency and develop his personal style and motifs- whether that's visual elements like the light synthesizer or gameplay mechanics like the assist droid. In a landscape of further consolidation and commodification in the video game industry, this is a tribute to a true independent spirit and a testament to true artistry.

I'm all in on the Gold Master Series stuff from Digital Eclipse. After The Making of Karateka and now Llamasoft: The Jeff Minter Story, I'll grab any of these.

There's something really fun and exciting about playing a developer's games from the very beginning - a crude Centipede knock off for the Spectrum to a psychedelic Tempest sequel for the Jaguar. You can see Minter's voice and vision clarify over a decade, and you get bits and pieces of who he is from documentary snippets from a forthcoming film, and photography, notes to himself, and fun quotables. 

Comparing this with the previous game in this series, where Jordan Mechner is a guy who worked extremely hard on a handful of games, Jeff Minter was in the practice of programming a game in a week and sending it out into the world. You couldn't have picked two more different guys to profile, other than that their initials are the same.

Great, weird, fun and all the additional context and background they provide - and the work they do to make the emulated games play nice on a game pad - lets you enjoy the games for what they are instead of weird old puzzles you noodle with for 30 seconds.

Digital Eclipse makes some of the best documentary-styled compilations of games, and this is no exception. If you like the history of video games and learning about designers while also getting to try some of these pieces for yourself without having to resort to tracking down physical copies, you'll like Llamasoft: The Jeff Minter Story.

That being said, his games are not for everyone's tastes. You'll enjoy them if you like light shows (do NOT buy this if you have Epilepsy), animals, and arcade-styled score chasing games. It has all those things in spades, the best of which being Tempest 2000, which I found very hard to put down. 

Jeff's games are one thing, but his relaxed (very British) personality is another. He really is someone who perseveres, found his audience and brought them along with him on his creative journey. I found the documentary clips inspiring, entertaining, and the overall presentation package very well-done.

8.5/10, I think this Gold Master series is really fantastic!

At the end of the day it is a $10 game, but the developer just didn't implement so many easy improvements that would have dramatically increased the quality of the game, so I cannot recommend it in its current state.

review_text_for_llm:
The game features a spectacular mechanic that allows players to create a centipede using various equipment to buff their units and deploy units to deal damage to enemies. The positioning of these units also influences the outcome of each wave, as buffs only affect the nearest units. This adds a strategic element, requiring players to plan and position their units carefully to create a powerful centipede.

However, my main challenge with the game lies in its movement mechanics. As the centipede grows, controlling its movement becomes increasingly difficult.

For future updates, I would like to suggest the following:

Introduce new achievements. A game of this kind benefits greatly from having a wide variety of achievements to keep players engaged and motivated.

Consider adding permanent upgrades. This could provide players with a sense of progression and a lasting impact on their centipede-building experience.

Bought this because I saw an ad for it on Reddit. I'm very mad that my algorithm knows me this well, but I am also very glad that it led me to this game.

Anyway, based on screenshots, you might think it's a single-player Overcooked. It's more of a management game than anything else. Gameplay in the kitchen involves preparing different meals at different stations (frying pan, pot, meat station, veggies, etc.) and managing the cooks who can move from station to station. You get better quality points if more cooks are involved in the cooking process of each meal, and you get combo points if cooks alternate steps in cooking. Getting into the rhythm of the gameplay, "tossing" meals across stations to different cooks, is very fun and satisfying thanks to the little audio and visual prompts that accompany each completed step of cooking. 

Timing plays a huge part in how well you perform in each level. The game provides a customizable auto-pause feature to help you manage where your dishes should go next. I often relied on auto-pause in the very early levels but found that supplementing that with manual pausing greatly increased how efficient I was with my time and my cooks' positioning.

review_text_for_llm:
Hidden gem of a cooking game with relationship and romance elements!!!

I'm not sure if it opens up to more chefs, but where I am in the game, you cook in pairs. The relationship system is somehwat similar to Fire Emblem (C, B, A, and S rank only for romantic partners) where they rank up as you pair them together. You do NOT have to choose the main character in the pairing, which is always fun. There are lots of fun platonic pair-ups too!

There are main and side missions, but you are kind of shoe-horned down one main path with your choices of who to recruit and use along the way. There are also really short relationship-boosting mini game missions, like hiking or fishing, where you can boost relationships between MC and other characters.

It might not be clear from screenshots, but you can pause during cooking segments -- there are segments where one person might work faster while someone idles for a second, but it's more or less turn based.

If you itch for games with relationship systems and crafting like me... you'll find a really solid one in Kitchen Sync Aloha!

It's a good game, but I wouldn't 100% it like the first game. The maps are far bigger than the first game but the scanner radius hasn't enlarged enough to compensate. So you'd be running across each map for dozens of minutes and still miss stuff. While late game items do help, they don't make it seamless like the first game. And the secrets are sometimes so convoluted that it really isn't possible to figure them out unless you're using an external guide

But I'm still giving this a positive rating, because these are only issues if you try to 100% the game. For a casual playthrough it's blast. But still play the first game if you haven't, as this game expects you to carry over the mechanic lessons from the first one. And if you like the first one, you'll like the second one. But beware if you decide to 100% the game you'll be in for a grind. 

And a message for the dev, please add some more endgame tools for 100% the game. Mainly a larger scanner tool for the remaining collectables, and have the decompiler be affected by the infinite ammo potion. Because trying to do these solo without external guides is really tedious. Like a buff to the snake oil would be perfect. I only ask this

This game has you going to different "dimensions," and then running around doing quests. Each quest has a reward of some type, but most of them don't really feel... rewarding. There are armored trains and railway guns! You can run over enemy tanks with your trains if you time it right.

What is really impressive is that the game is about 900mb in size. you don't notice it when you play it as if it were a game with >4gb in large.

Some complaints:
Why does money have invincibility frames when spawning AND flies all over the place? A lot of cash just flies off somewhere where you can't collect it and it's generally annoying to go fetch some coins that flew really far away.
Please let me rebind the keys for changing spells and weapons.

[h1]Experienced on the Meta Quest 3[/h1]

You can view my gameplay & early impressions here: https://youtu.be/3JIdxR2eOYA

This may be a good game, but I am reviewing the VR experience only. Unfortunately, the VR support is very basic at the moment. The game is way too dark on my VR headset (Meta Quest 3) and the brightness setting seemed to only affect the desktop view.

Quirky game full of personality, the dialogue and story is just wonderfully quirky and amusing.

Unfortunately it does need a LOT of balancing changes, right now it's just way too easy and uninvolved, my character can defeat almost any enemy in a single hit, including boss battles, and the only way she gets hit is if she misses.

I feel like both the enemies and my character should deal less damage overall so that fights have some stakes to them, with my hero's health slowly being chipped as they go through their quest. 

The hero care sections could also use some work, right now there is no reason not to simply buy a ton of coffee and other stat healing items and completely forego letting them sleep, bath, use the bathroom, etc. Money is just too abundant, especially on chapter 2. I finished like 5 missions and money became competely obsolete.

In summary, this game has a lot of potential, its skeleton is solid as it is, it's a fun little game to leave open while doing other tasks much like an actual tamagotchi. But I really hope it gets some extra TLC from the devs to help it achieve its full potential

review_text_for_llm:
This is a very good pro football simulation, probably the best one on the market now. It is NOT a joystick action game, but instead allows you to be the GM and/or coach of an NFL type team. You draft the players, sign free agents, stay within a salary cap, take your team through training camp, pre-season, and the regular season all the way to the league championship game if you're good enough. You can even call the offensive and defensive plays within a game and the results are very realistic.

There is an abundance of statistics and they are realistic. You can play with real NFL players or use fictional players. You can even start your league with a 53 round draft if you wish. Scouts and coaches are hired and fired by you.

My only 'gripe' is that there is as yet no way to print the games' output like there used to be in FOF 8. 

All in all, if you like American football and relish the challenge of setting up and coaching an NFL type team with real or fictional players you'll love this game.

Finally, there is a robust FOF9 community developing add-ons such as logos and player photos. It's really the only worthwhile serious sim of its type.

[h2] A Lady in Red Crosses Your Way Late One Night... [/h2]
Japanese horror is a sub-genre of the horror genre that I genuinely find some fear in. Things like Chilla’s Arts' games, [i]Ringu[/i], and [i]Ju-On[/i] put me on edge. However, even though I am terrified by these examples, I still appreciate them and J-horror. I noticed one game released recently in this sub-genre, so I had to check it out.

In [i]Akai Onna[/i], you play as a student walking home late one night when a strange woman in red walks past you. A man also runs by that night, but you don’t think much of it. A few nights later, a police officer asked us if we’d seen anyone suspicious and informed us of an incident three nights prior. I won’t spoil the rest of the game, but the student’s life will never be the same again.

This game feels less like a game and more like a kaleidoscope of dreams. 

It is really hard to describe the gameplay. Basically, you wander through a set of randomly filled worlds by randomly generated doors. Disillusion ST is a little less random that it may appear at the first glance but when you will find some correlations they will be barely useful.

Because of that, the game may feel really disappointing or even annoying if you are playing it just like a regular game. It gives you a goal – find all the artifacts. But if you ever try to focus on one, you will rapidly fall into a spiral of frustration. Every interaction, every battle, every door will feel like an obstacle that pushes you far away from your target. You are not going to achieve anything if you play Disillusion ST like a regular game.

Instead, you should let it go, give up, and just go with the flow of the game. Counterintuitively, only when you have no intention of making any progress at all, the puzzle pieces will start clipping into the places. The only way to walk through the game is to wander through. At the moment you realize this, you will find 15-20 hours of your life have disappeared.

Typing of the Dead, but with an adventure Resident Evil style to it. The game has a lot of charm to it and presents a nice level of challenges to choose from, both for the typing speed and the game in general. I found that the default setting was just right when going into this as a new player. 

You do everything simply with the keyboard. You move around by typing short word, with some longer ones and phrases for doors and objectives. You shot/smack the enemies by typing. You heal by typing to consume and/or mix food. It takes a bit of time to get used, and you shouldn't forget to simply put some distance between you and the enemies, and not simply face tank everything. 

There are a fair number of characters with abilities and stat differences to choose from, and the game is episodic. That said, I played the first map co-op first time and then replayed solo and there is some randomization to how things are laid out in the level. So while the main quest is the same, it presents some replay value if you wanna push the difficulty up and go again. 

Overall, liking it so far, and hope they keep adding episodes! Thumbs up!

Honestly it's really hecking fun, and a very, very good game for $10. What makes it so special is that it's not a Typing of the Dead ripoff; it's actually a Resident Evil ripoff, but with typing. It's not an arcade, light-gun style shooter. There's lots of planning and inventory management, including finding tapes to save your game, boarding up zones, and surviving waves of enemies every so often. What really surprised me is how well the weapons in this game are handled: they're all unique and have their own benefits, usually in the ways in which they alter what words you have to type (like how the flamethrower literally burns away the letters of the words, making you need to type less with each flame blast when using other weapons). There's about five hours of content to play through, give or take, across five randomised levels. The randomization has actually been surprisingly decent, to the point where I had actually thought the levels were static and hand-crafted the first couple of maps.
I've only been playing solo, as it requires room codes, so it's not really possible to play with random people at the moment, but it's been a good time in single player.

Blood Typers is a short but clever survival horror game that stands out with its unique typing-based mechanics. You don’t move around like in traditional games, which creates a sense of helplessness that adds to the tension. Almost every action (opening doors, fighting off enemies, or solving simple interactions) requires typing under pressure, making it genuinely spooky and immersive.

Interestingly, I found the easiest typing difficulty, "Beginner," to be harder than "Normal" because it throws strange, short combinations like “xes,” “gk,” and “xq” at you. Despite being shorter, these unfamiliar strings actually slowed me down more than full words.

There’s not a ton of content, but the idea is solid and the execution is fun. It feels like a passion project, simple but well thought out. If it were expanded into a longer game, I’d definitely spend more time with it. This kind of creative experimentation is exactly what the game industry could use more of. Definitely worth a try.

I really enjoy Typing of the Dead (TotD) on PC, but that hasn't received a proper update for modern PCs. Same goes for TotD 2 as well. At least TotD: Overkill is on Steam.

I also really enjoyed Blood Typers (BT) since it was the closest game to match TotD, while still being different on its own. BT is more of a survival horror game, while TotD is more of an arcade rail shooter. While I do enjoy TotD's progressive difficulty, I also enjoyed the various difficulty options BT offers, which is split between typing & survival difficulty. Now I like having the option of either quickly playing through one of BT's chapters, or committing an entire run through all six of TotD's chapters

There isn't a lot of content at the moment, with 4 out of 5 chapters currently available, yet I was perfectly okay with paying $10 to play another game in a relatively niche genre.

review_text_for_llm:
Blood Typers is a mashup of fantastic ideas that when brought together, give players something uniquely tense and frightening to play solo or with a group. If you're checking out this page, chances are you've played or at least know of Typing of the Dead. This game builds on the general gameplay feel of this title, but with one major twist: No auto-rail level designs, you control your character EXCLUSIVELY with your keyboard inputs. 

The trailers seem a bit hectic upon first watch, and trust me, the game can get hectic, too. But after diving into the game, the movement becomes fluid. You begin to glide through the different rooms and halls, remembering phrases and words to guide you to safety. The gameplay premise is pretty simple: collect 5 items, return those items to a specific location, and find the exit. I won't say more, because it's best experienced fresh.

This is an absolute must for any typing game lover, such a fresh take on the concept that. I am excited to continue exploring each Episode the game has currently to play and to see what else the team teleases in the future for the game.

review_text_for_llm:
Good game, very fun to type and kill. You wouldn't think so, but it actually makes it quite tense trying to land a hit when you're surrounded by lots of zombies, which makes it deliciously fun.
There's a couple of wrinkles in multiplayer that makes it a tad awkward: namely that, since all players share the same words when attacking, there's moments where two players will begin typing the same word but one finishes first, which causes their input characters to be "congested" with their attempted attack input and having to backspace.
These are small things, though, and I think easily fixable: even having a simple "clear" control that empties the text input would make it so much easier to coordinate with and play around other players.
All in all, a good, simple game that'll teach you to type for your life.

This is a really enjoyable PS1-esque arcade rally game. If you're coming here expecting ultra-realistic handling and physics, or the best graphics that money can buy, you'd be better off elsewhere as this just won't be what you're looking for. If you can accept those flaws, and approach the game for what it is rather than what you might want it to be, you'll have a great time.

I absolutely adore this game. I grew up playing things like Ridge Racer, Outrun, and numerous other titles in the arcades. But the one I always loved, that I would have given my spleen for, was my own cabinet version of Sega Rally. Is this game Sega Rally? No. Did it cost me my spleen? Also no. Does it give me that same thrill of a corner well taken, the perfect slide, the zig and zag of tight corners taken one after the other at high speed? Yes. Yes it does. 

It isn't perfect, the physics are... interesting, but by god it's fun. Sit down, grab that gamepad, and re-live those wonderful, loud, manic hours you spent in the arcade as a kid, trying again and again to get that one last race in before your money ran out, or you had to go home. Also, the soundtrack is absolutely banging. 

This is genuinely the best money I have spent on a video game since I was 16 years old, smacking 50 pence pieces into a cigarette stinking arcade machine, on a cold blustery day down on the English coast, while my bored grandparents moaned about the "price of fish and chips these days".

Buy it.

Old School Rally is a game in which the title tells you virtually everything you may need to know on a surface level. Inspired by rally games from the mid to late nineties, Old School Rally aims to capture and recreate the gameplay and aesthetics of its contemporaries dating back to the fifth generation of console gaming, as well as arcade games that were available at that time.

The graphics are a wonderful example of how aesthetics can induce nostalgia. Be expecting boxy models, with low resolution textures, dithering in place of shading, and periodic model and texture warping to simulate a certain console's integer based rendering scheme. The environments do look the part when compared to older games, however set pieces on the track do become repetitive after a while. Fitting for the era that Old School Rally is trying to emulate, but would have appreciated a bit more visual diversity.

Cars respond with snappy, slightly exaggerated physics, prioritizing responsiveness and momentum rather than authentic tire modeling or weight dynamics.
