Story (if you can say there is any) is suggested at through some overlays and audio clips displayed on the screen mid-game, and honestly none of them are creepy or fitting at all.  They're all just kind of goofy.

Overall would not recommend at or near full price.  I would say wait to see if it ever drops to about $3 or so in the future.

I really wanted to like this game because the creator said it was partially inspired by House of Leaves which I love, and I generally like slow-burn, slow paced walking sim type indie games. 

This game is *fine*, it does a few things well enough. It gives the player quite a few interesting ways of interacting with objects, though none of them are really necessary aside from grab and throw. You can kick objects around if you want, which you can use to your advantage to move bigger items while you are carrying boxes. Endo 2 is an interesting game, because it elevates the first one so much, but it doesn't turn it irrelevant. This entry is harder but the levels are briefer as well.

The new inventory system is both a blessing and a curse: A blessing because it allows for more flexible play, and having the items placement be freeform is not only fun, but allows for planning. And a curse because it's more overbearing - having to reach your backpack, pressing the button to quit the menu... the first game's system was definitely more intuitive.

I enjoy the visual leap as well, with really cool looking 3D environments and props, and a smoother looking fog. The simple visuals of the characters paired up with the detailed props and illustrations make quite a contrast, and it's highly accessible game just due to that.

I know the game has been released and making a wishlist for it is stupid, but I just wished the game could be better, but it's just ok.

Endoparasitic 1, 9/10
Endoparasitic 2, 6/10

Good sequel, but it stands on similar footing to the original when you compare the improvements, and its drawbacks.

It adds enough to make the concept feel fresh, but I was hoping for a bit more variety by the end of the game, there are only really 5 enemy types, one of which is an alternate version of the basic enemy, 2 weapons, and 1 somewhat useful tool. And they all replace the original weapons.

All the levels are a repeat of the same formula, getting off an elevator, finding a button to unlock the next floor, and going back to the elevator. It could have been spiced up a bit more, add different objectives or alternate paths between floors, something like that.

Good game though. The ending felt a bit anticlimactic, and it felt like more of a sequel hook than the original.

Looking quite simple at the beginning Rebel Rush is a suprisingly deep pazzle game which will make you want to challenge yourself more more in finding ways to reach the golden snitch cup split-seconds faster. Yes, you heard it right - it is not a racing game - it is a platformer/pazzle where not only speed, but precision, timing and planning gives you the best result.

I have caught myeself multiple times grinning with excitment when I managed to find new and more effective way to reach the finish while exploring futuristic Gastown and poking my nose in every corner of a racing map.


And when you will finally manage to outrun your own ghost you will rightfully take your place at the ladderboard ... only to see that some bastard took the first place with the result of 23 microseconds faster than yours. That is where you start to desperatly feel the urge to go and try again because you know that you could do better!


Tails Noir characters narative between the maps is a nice little touch to spice things up.


I was waiting for the release of the game with excitment and would recommend everyone to give it a try!

The only downside here is the somewhat bad pronunciation and that the subtitles do not always match what is heard (or simply some sentences are skipped).

Sorting clothes, cleaning machines, and tackling quirky challenges keep things engaging—at least for a while. The grind, however, can get tedious. For speedrunners (which I am not), this is a must buy. For everyone else, definitely check it out if you enjoy these types of games.

Deeply atmospheric eldritch puzzle-hiking. unlike other "liminal space" games that obscure your paths from you, Blackshard lets you take in your whole environment to try to plan your routes at the same time as you take in the visual feast of truly massive panoramic scenery. Even though the levels feel massive it's never too frustrating to fall, or to backtrack to try a new route. There are many ways to get around a single map and not of them are straightforward in the least, letting you experiment and explore, which sometimes results in finding new secrets around corners you hadn't given thoughts to before!

The swapping between stark geometry and painterly, organic sculpture and character art makes a world that is at once decadent and stark, lonely but full of glimmering details. Addictive to explore, wondrous to behold, and gives you just enough to get wrapped up in both the warnings and pleadings of the plot.

The weakness of most incremental games is how quickly they become repetitive, there's only so long you can watch numbers go up before they lose all their meaning. Snakecremental avoids this by grounding the upgrades in the gameplay of Snake. You can have all the upgrades in the game, but you ultimately still need to be good at Snake.

The upgrades also feel impactful, which is essential for a game like this. Unlocking red health pips and blue armor pips genuinely changes the way you approach the game. Figuring out whether to conserve health and prolong the game or live fast and pick up the rare materials is an interesting decision.

But ultimately, the gameplay is still just Snake with a little extra sauce. I beat the game in 4 hours and even then it felt a bit like it overstayed its welcome. Still, in a world where everything is trying to monopolize your time and money, $4 for 4 hours of fun, mindless gamplay is a pretty great deal.

In classic snake, the optimal strategy is just slowly slither trough the map in a predetermined zig-zag pattern to make sure you get all the pellets and never eat your tail. But here that's sub-optimal, forcing you to actually snake around in all sorts of interesting ways, optimizing between getting health, getting armor, making sure you stack up as many greens as possible to get the highest multiplier imaginable as you go all out and get the higher tier pellets to fully max out your score. It really diverts from the classic snake game to make you go for "riskier" maneuvers and rewards you for it.

it really is truly genius. Don't be deceived, from the outside it looks like just another boring "what if classic game but tech tree incremental". But it honestly does a lot more than just smash the two together. The mechanics of both of these massively compliment each other creating a game that truly is way greater than the sum of its parts.

Since neutral scores aren't possible, I'll give this a qualified thumbs up.

The concept is great if perhaps not entirely realized, the gameplay at times is solid, and the price point is mostly reasonable to take a flyer on it.

The downsides, however, are here. Progressing through Red and Blue is pretty smooth. Green starts to chug a little. Yellow...ouch.  

This is made a bit worse by two factors, I think: 
1) Within each run you still need to collect red (for a chance at health restoration) and blue (to increase armor) to have an effective run, and to boost your overall multiplier for that run, even if you've largely exhausted upgrades from those colors.  In theory that need to balance multiple colors SHOULD keep runs fresh, however
2) There is a large RNG component, so you could do two runs effectively "the same" and see wildly different results.

It's a game I really want to love, but instead after about 75 min it's shifted to "liking in a very small doses."  I'll do a few runs a day and decide that's enough.  Will I ever 100% this?  Eh, probably not.
